item.text: I’ve reviewed the earlier rows from memory and identified additional specific parallels, especially thirst, bitter liquids, vessel containment, and reciprocal exhortation. I’m saving only those new proposals.

item.command:
/bin/bash -lc "cat > enrichment/bible/work/s103/discovery/s103-20261009/sec3/luna/followup.tsv <<'EOF'
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Lam.4.4	Tongue of the infant clings from thirst	The commentary names a thirst-dried tongue as maʿṣūr; in Jerusalem's siege the infant's tongue clings to the palate for thirst, making the bodily image concrete in a scene of deprivation.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Isa.41.17	Tongue fails for thirst; water is promised	The needy have no water and their tongue fails from thirst; this closely matches the commentary's dried tongue, while Isaiah's promised springs reverse depletion with relief.
strong	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Prov.30.16	Commentary label root ع ص ر; Hebrew עצר, table sound correspondence only	The proverb names the closed womb with עצר; this table correspondence links the commentary's root to bodily closure, while the proverb's unsatisfied earth and water add a distinct thirst setting.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Prov.30.16	Closed womb and earth unsatisfied with water	The proverb places a closed womb beside earth that is never satisfied with water; this meets the commentary's closure and thirst images together, but as unsated lack rather than a bottle retaining medicine.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Num.5.24	Bitter water that brings a curse	The suspected woman is made to drink water of bitterness that brings a curse; this is a concrete counter-use of bitter liquid beside the commentary's bitter plant extract called medicine.
medium	tevrat	karsi_anlati	WLC:Num.5.27	Bitter water brings bodily affliction	The ritual's consequence is that the water becomes bitter within the woman and brings a curse; bitterness here exposes and punishes rather than healing as in the commentary's medicinal sabr.
medium	tevrat	karsi_anlati	WLC:Lam.3.15	Bitterness and wormwood as affliction	The speaker says he has been filled with bitterness and wormwood; the plant bitterness is imposed misery, a counter-reading to the commentary's painful but beneficial remedy.
strong	incil	karsi_anlati	SBLGNT:Rev.8.11	Wormwood makes waters bitter and kills many	The star named Wormwood makes the waters bitter and many die from them; this directly reverses the commentary's bitter plant extract as medicine by making bitter liquid lethal.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Rev.10.9	Scroll sweet in the mouth, bitter in the stomach	John is told to eat the scroll, which will be sweet in his mouth but bitter in his stomach; the two-stage taste gives the commentary's swallowed bitter medicine a distinct prophetic counterpart.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Rev.10.10	Sweet taste turns bitter after eating	John reports that the scroll tasted sweet and then made his stomach bitter; this locates bitterness after ingestion, unlike the commentary's bitter extract whose bitterness is already the medicinal quality.
medium	incil	karsi_anlati	SBLGNT:Matt.27.34	Wine mixed with gall is offered and refused	Jesus is offered wine mixed with gall and refuses it after tasting; this gives a specific bitter drink in a suffering scene, but the text presents no healing benefit like the commentary's medicine.
weak	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Mark.15.23	Wine mixed with myrrh is refused	Mark says wine mixed with myrrh is offered to Jesus and he does not take it; the plant resin in a wine drink recalls the commentary's plant-derived bitter essence, though Mark does not call it bitter or medicinal.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:John.19.28	Jesus says he thirsts	At the crucifixion Jesus says he thirsts; this is a specific bodily thirst scene beside the commentary's dried tongue, with the speaker's impending death making the need unresolved.
strong	incil	karsi_anlati	SBLGNT:John.19.29	Sour wine lifted to the thirsty Jesus	The bystanders raise sour wine to Jesus after he says he thirsts; the drink is acidic relief in a death scene, not the beneficial bitter remedy described in the commentary.
strong	incil	karsi_anlati	SBLGNT:Mark.2.22	New wine bursts wineskins	Jesus says new wine put into old wineskins bursts them and both wine and skins are lost; unlike the commentary's corked bottle retaining a medicinal essence, this vessel fails under pressure and causes loss.
strong	incil	karsi_anlati	SBLGNT:Rev.14.19	Earth's grapes thrown into the winepress of wrath	The angel gathers the earth's grapes and throws them into God's great winepress; this directly turns the commentary's pressing that yields good essence into an apocalyptic harvest of wrath.
strong	incil	karsi_anlati	SBLGNT:Rev.14.20	Winepress trodden; blood flows out	The press is trodden outside the city and blood flows from it; this specifies the destructive yield of the preceding winepress, in contrast to the commentary's useful extracted juice.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:1Kgs.17.14	Jar of meal and jug of oil do not fail during drought	Elijah promises that the widow's jar and jug will not be emptied until rain returns; the contained provision in scarcity parallels the commentary's stored essence and its Yusuf scene of relief after famine.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:1Kgs.17.16	The jar and jug remain supplied	The narrative says the widow's jar and jug did not fail as promised; this continuation shows stored liquid and food sustaining life through drought, unlike a one-time extracted dose.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:2Kgs.4.6	Oil fills every borrowed vessel and then stops	The widow's oil keeps filling containers until there is no vessel left, when the flow stops; it gives a precise parallel to liquid collected and held by a vessel, with provision released rather than a corked medicine.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Amos.9.13	Treader of grapes overtaken by the sower; hills drip wine	Amos pictures restoration so abundant that grape-treading overlaps sowing and mountains drip sweet wine; this makes pressing the sign of relief and plenty, as in the commentary's post-scarcity year.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Judg.6.11	Gideon threshes wheat in a winepress to hide it	Gideon works grain in a winepress while hiding from Midianite raiders; the press belongs to threatened subsistence here, unlike the commentary's press as the sign that scarcity has ended.
strong	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Ps.34.11	Commentary label root خ س ر; Hebrew חסר, table sound correspondence only	The verse says young lions lack and hunger while those who seek YHWH lack no good thing; Hebrew חסר gives the commentary's decrease a direct cognate contrast between want and provision.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Col.3.12	Put on patience with other virtues	Paul tells the community to put on compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness, and patience; this places patience among shared ethical dispositions, extending the commentary's community defined by sabr.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Col.3.13	Bear with and forgive one another	The addressees are told to bear with and forgive one another; this gives the commentary's mutual counsel in patience a concrete practice of forbearance.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Col.3.16	Teach and admonish one another with the word	Paul tells the community to teach and admonish one another with wisdom as Christ's word dwells among them; this is a close communal counterpart to mutual counsel in truth.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Thess.5.14	Admonish, encourage, help, and be patient with all	Paul urges the church to admonish the idle, encourage the fainthearted, help the weak, and be patient with everyone; this combines mutual moral care with patience in concrete cases.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Thess.5.15	Seek the good of one another and everyone	The church must not repay evil for evil but always pursue good for one another and all; this connects reciprocal ethical counsel to doing good.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:2Tim.2.24	The Lord's servant must be patient and able to teach	Paul describes the Lord's servant as not quarrelsome but patient and able to teach; this joins patient conduct to truthful instruction, though it is pastoral rather than reciprocal.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:2Tim.2.25	Correct opponents gently toward knowledge of truth	The servant is to correct opponents gently in hope that God grants them knowledge of truth; this directly joins correction and truth, adding a one-directional teaching scene to the commentary's mutual counsel.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:James.2.14	Can faith without works save? 	James asks whether a person who claims faith but has no works can be saved; this directly tests the commentary's pairing of belief and righteous action, making their relation explicit.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:James.2.17	Faith without works is dead	James says faith without works is dead; this gives a specific Christian account of why belief and deeds belong together in the commentary's exception from loss.
strong	incil	karsi_anlati	SBLGNT:Rom.2.8	Disobedience to truth brings wrath	Paul contrasts those who obey truth with those who disobey truth and pursue unrighteousness, who receive wrath; this counters the commentary's mutual truth-counsel by depicting refusal of truth as a path to judgment.
strong	incil	karsi_anlati	SBLGNT:Luke.9.24	Losing life for Jesus saves it	Jesus says the one who loses life for his sake will save it; this reverses the commentary's general human loss into a paradoxical self-loss that leads to rescue.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:James.1.12	Enduring trial leads to the crown of life	James calls blessed the person who endures trial and promises the crown of life; this connects patience under pressure to a salvific outcome.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Pet.1.7	Tested faith compared with refined gold	Peter says tested faith, more precious than perishable gold refined by fire, will result in praise and honor; this gives pressure a refining yield, though by fire rather than squeezing.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:John.15.2	Pruning a fruitful branch for more fruit	Jesus says the vinedresser prunes the fruitful branch so it bears more fruit; this gives the commentary's grape and pressure images a contrasting cultivation model where cutting increases future yield.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Matt.26.39	Jesus asks that the cup pass, then submits	Jesus asks whether the cup can pass but submits to the Father's will; the cup makes suffering a drink-like burden, while the scene adds willing endurance rather than the commentary's extracted medicine.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Matt.26.42	Jesus accepts the cup he must drink	Jesus says that if the cup cannot pass unless he drinks it, the Father's will be done; this continuation turns the cup from a requested escape into accepted suffering.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:2Cor.9.10	God supplies seed and increases the harvest of righteousness	Paul uses seed, bread, and an increased harvest of righteousness; this connects agricultural yield to the commentary's good essence and gives generosity an ethical harvest image.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:2Cor.9.11	Enrichment for generosity	Paul says the community is enriched in every way for generosity; this closely matches the commentary's report that expressed juice serves as a figure for goodness and giving.
medium	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Prov.30.16	Commentary label root ع ص ر; Hebrew עצר, table sound correspondence only	The proverb's closed womb uses the Hebrew root the table matches to Arabic ع ص ر; it supplies a bodily use of closure distinct from pressing and from the bottle-stopper sense in the commentary.
EOF"
